summary: An experimental document that takes a broad look at distributed printing and lists real-life scenarios that clarify the features needed in an Internet printing protocol. It identifies requirements for end users, operators and administrators.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2567 sets out what people and organizations need from printing over the Internet. It describes the goals and scenarios that the Internet Printing Protocol documents address.

subtitle: A set of design goals and scenarios for printing across networks and organizations.

tldr.problem: Remote printing involves finding a printer, installing its driver, sending a job, checking its status, and handling security across different networks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists needs for end users, operators, and administrators, then describes protocol objectives and example printing scenarios. Only some end-user goals are planned for IPP/1.0.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2567 is an Experimental requirements document. Its IESG note says a later standards-track version was expected to differ from this memo.

sections.title: Where This Memo Fits
sections.content:
Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing with Internet tools. This memo is one part of a document set describing IPP and focuses on printing needs and examples rather than defining the full protocol.

The memo says IPP/1.0 focuses on end-user functions. Operator and administrator needs are outside that version's scope. The IESG note warns that the expected standards-track revision may change the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo describes the goals for printing over the Internet. It focuses on what people who send print jobs need from the first version of IPP.

sections.title: Printers, Drivers, and Configurations
sections.content:
Internet printing means using Internet tools to print to a remote printer after initial setup, using methods similar to printing locally. A printer is any device that marks media. A driver is client-side code that creates the data stream for a printer; driver installation and the protocol between a server and printer are outside IPP's scope.

The memo describes clients talking either to a printer built into one device or to a server that represents one or more physical printers. In each configuration, the user sees a Printer object.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPP client can contact a printer directly or contact a server that represents a printer. The user works with one printer entry even when a server manages the physical device.

sections.title: Goals for Users and Administrators
sections.content:
End users need to find printers by name, location, or capability; check status and capabilities; submit jobs; see job status; and cancel their jobs. A job may come from an application, a file sent with the request, or a document referenced by a URI. Users may also set job properties such as copies, sides, finishing, and priority.

Operators monitor printers, respond to problems, and may manage jobs. Administrators create printer entries and manage authorization and billing. The memo marks operator and administrator functions as not required for IPP/1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Users need to find printers, send jobs, check progress, and cancel their own jobs. The first IPP version does not require the listed operator and administrator functions.

sections.title: Protocol Objectives
sections.content:
The protocol should work across client and server operating systems. It must handle print data created as an application produces it as well as data that is stored before sending, without making the difference visible to the user.

The memo calls for extensibility, version negotiation, internationalization, and the ability to pass through firewalls or proxy servers when administrators allow it. It does not require backward compatibility with LPD, but calls for a mapping that can support an LPD-to-IPP gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP is intended to work across different operating systems and printing methods. It should allow extensions and firewall traversal, while a separate mapping can connect it to LPD.

sections.title: Printing Scenarios
sections.content:
The scenarios describe printer discovery, driver installation, job submission, status and capability checks, notifications, and cancellation. They are protocol-neutral examples; the memo does not say that every function belongs in IPP/1.0.

A printer must respond to each print request with information about success or failure. The protocol must support files sent with the job, data generated during submission, and files referenced by a URI. It must also account for printer overruns and devices that print while data is still arriving.
sections.plainLanguage: The scenarios show how a person can find a printer, send a job, follow its status, receive a notice, or cancel it. Each job request receives a response.

sections.title: Security and Driver Installation
sections.content:
The protocol must be able to operate in secure environments and should reuse existing security protocols where reasonable. The memo identifies data-origin authentication, privacy, integrity, and non-repudiation as message-protection goals. Requirements may differ because the client, printer, and document can belong to different security domains.

Installing a printer driver can expose a computer to defective, malicious, or inappropriate software. The memo says administrators should configure downloads so they can verify the software's source and protect the software during transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Print jobs may need protection because the client, printer, and document can be in different security domains. Driver downloads should let administrators verify the source and protect the software.
